articles.title: Debate na Globo: a reação da mãe de Ana Clara | G1
articles.standfirst: Cristiane Gomes da Silva estava na plateia a convite do petista. O candidato do PL errou seu nome e foi chamado de mentiroso. Convidados de Flávio gritaram para ela calara a boca.
articles.summary: Cristiane Gomes da Silva, mãe da menina Ana Clara, chamou Flávio Bolsonaro de mentiroso após ser mandada calar a boca por aliados do senador no debate da Globo.
articles.body:
Um dos momentos mais tensos do debate presidencial da TV Globo foi quando Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) perguntou para Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) sobre a morte da menina Ana Clara, aos 5 anos, durante uma operação policial em Niterói, em 2021. O candidato do PL é advogado do militar suspeito de atirar com fuzil no peito da garota. A mãe de Ana Clara, Cristiane Gomes da Silva, estava na plateia a convite da campanha do petista.

Lula perguntou: "O que leva um senador a defender um policial que deu um tiro de fuzil numa menina de cinco anos? "Que território é esse? O território da bala?"

E quando Flávio respondia que era "um território dominado por esses narcoterroristas", Cristiane balança a cabeça em negação e o chama de mentiroso.

Depois, Flávio a chama pelo nome da filha. Cristiane grita: "ela morreu".

Do lado outro lado da plateia, convidados de Flávio pedem silêncio.

Cristiane continua falando baixo, enquanto escuta a resposta do senador e novamente o chama de "mentiroso". Mais uma vez, escuta pedidos de silêncio vindo do outro lado da plateia.

Quando Flávio diz que vai "ajudar" a saber "quem foi o autor" do tiro, a mulher reclama e volta a chamar o candidato de mentiroso. Desta vez, aliados de Flávio gritam: "cala a boca".

Enquanto Flávio continua a dar sua resposta, Cristiane mantém uma atitude de negar as falas do candidato, balançando a cabeça com indignação.

Ao final do debate, em um vídeo publicado por "O Globo", a mãe de Ana Clara diz que o candidato não respondeu à pergunta que ela queria escutar. Além disso, denunciou que a Polícia já sabe quem atirou e que o julgamento só não aconteceu porque Flávio teria agido para adiar.

Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula no estúdio do debate desta sexta-feira (23) — Foto: Globo/Manoella Mello

articles.title: Urnas são distribuídas em Macaé, Rio das Ostras e Casimiro | G1
articles.standfirst: Urnas já foram distribuídas e cidades terão esquema especial para o segundo turno; transporte público será gratuito para facilitar o deslocamento dos eleitores.
articles.summary: Urnas já foram distribuídas e cidades terão esquema especial para o segundo turno; transporte público será gratuito para facilitar o deslocamento dos eleitores.
articles.body:
As urnas eletrônicas que serão utilizadas no segundo turno das eleições começaram a ser distribuídas neste sábado (24) em Macaé , no Norte Fluminense, e nos municípios de Rio das Ostras e Casimiro de Abreu , na Baixada Litorânea do Rio.

Os equipamentos estão sendo levados para os locais de votação com apoio das forças de segurança e ficarão sob vigilância até a abertura das seções, neste domingo (25). Juntos, os três municípios somam 329.021 eleitores aptos a votar.

Além da logística para o transporte das urnas, as três cidades terão transporte público gratuito no dia da votação para facilitar o deslocamento dos eleitores aos locais de votação.

Macaé tem 185.795 eleitores aptos a votar. Ao todo, serão utilizadas 559 urnas em 84 locais de votação, além de 44 urnas de contingência, destinadas à substituição de equipamentos em caso de necessidade.

No primeiro turno, 41.744 eleitores não compareceram às urnas, o que representa uma abstenção de 22,47%. O transporte público municipal será gratuito, das 6h às 19h . A medida vale para todos os usuários, inclusive para quem utiliza o Cartão Macaé, que não precisará ser apresentado no embarque.

Em Rio das Ostras, 107.154 eleitores estão aptos a votar . O município contará com 340 urnas eletrônicas, sendo 316 destinadas às seções eleitorais e 24 de contingência. A distribuição dos equipamentos para os 38 locais de votação, divididos em 15 áreas, foi realizada neste sábado com escolta policial.

No primeiro turno, 24.758 eleitores não compareceram às urnas, o equivalente a 23,11% do eleitorado. Não houve alteração nos locais de votação em relação ao primeiro turno.

Já em Casimiro de Abreu, 36.072 eleitores estão aptos a votar . O município contará com 126 urnas eletrônicas, das quais 117 serão utilizadas nas seções eleitorais e nove ficarão como contingência.

O transporte dos equipamentos foi realizado neste sábado em ônibus escolares cedidos pela prefeitura. As urnas foram levadas aos locais de votação com escolta da Polícia Militar e permanecerão sob vigilância da PM e da Guarda Municipal durante a noite.

O serviço Primaveras, que já opera sem cobrança de tarifa, terá os horários de circulação divulgados pela prefeitura, incluindo trajetos entre Barra de São João, a sede do município e a região serrana.

No primeiro turno, 8.262 eleitores não compareceram às urnas em Casimiro de Abreu, uma abstenção de 22,90%.

Os equipamentos estão sendo levados para os locais de votação com apoio das forças de segurança; juntos, os três municípios somam 329.021 eleitores aptos a votar. — Foto: Lavínia Torres

articles.title: Republican billionaire Rick Jackson is walking a Trump tightrope in his quest to lead Georgia
articles.summary: ATLANTA (AP) — He's hardly the first billionaire to promise working-class voters he'll fight for them in public office. Rick Jackson, the Republican candidat...
articles.body:
ATLANTA (AP) — He's hardly the first billionaire to promise working-class voters he'll fight for them in public office. Rick Jackson , the Republican candidate for Georgia governor, has even compared himself to the real estate mogul who reached the Oval Office.

But Jackson's path differs from Donald Trump's , and the 72-year-old healthcare magnate and investor brings a vastly different persona to his first campaign. Unlike Trump, who was born to wealth , Jackson spent his early years bouncing through foster homes before launching his first company as a young man.

Now, he wants to leverage both his similarities and contrasts with the president, a challenge he's tackling with buckets of his own campaign cash and a personal story that anchors his appeal to voters.

"I have lived in poverty," Jackson says. "When you have not eaten, you never forget that, and you don't forget the people that are struggling."

Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms , a former Atlanta mayor, disputes Jackson's altruistic pitch, setting up the Nov. 3 election as a test of whether an alternate, softer version of conservative billionaire politics can complement or even counter Trump's pugilistic populism in a key swing state.

Jackson planned to join Trump at a rally Saturday in Perry, in what would be his second appearance with the president in the closing stretch of the campaign.

"My father left me at nine months old. My mother was a sixth-grade educated waitress with a severe alcohol problem," Jackson said in the only debate of their general election campaign. "I had seven stepfathers before I was 12. I lived in the projects, went to 13 different schools, and lived in five different foster homes."

He left college to start a business at 21. That led to Jackson Healthcare, a behemoth company that provides contract nurses and other workers to hospitals and health systems, including public entities that have helped fuel Jackson's fortunes with taxpayer money.

At events with supporters, Jackson gets more personal.

"I have, because of my background, severe abandonment issues," he told hundreds of voters in Cleveland, a conservative enclave in the north Georgia mountains. He turns that acknowledgment into a promise: "Let me tell you one thing: I will never abandon you."

Rags-to-riches themes are not uncommon in politics, and it's yielded Jackson's campaign motto: "From foster care to billionaire." But the scale is eye-popping, illuminated by the nearly $200 million Jackson has spent personally on the campaign. That puts him among the largest self-funding candidates in the history of American elections.

But on that score, too, Jackson tries to soften the caricature of the billionaire executive.

"It's not my money," he said in a northern suburb of Atlanta. Jackson calls his fortune "God's money" and says that "my job is to have kingdom impact" with it.

"The reason I have spent so much money to do this," he said, is to "help 11 million Georgians, to keep them from struggling."

Jackson launched his bid as a relative unknown, though Capitol insiders knew him because of Jackson Healthcare, its lucrative state contracts and his lobbying interest in healthcare, business and tax policy.

The Republican primary field featured a trio of statewide elected officials, including Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who won Trump's endorsement in August 2025 , before Jackson got in.

During the primary, Jackson embraced the president even though he wasn't Trump's choice. Jackson sometimes promised to "be like Trump, but with Southern tone." He pledged to "deliver for Georgia the same type of business solutions that President Trump is bringing to our country."

Largely aligning himself with Trump on immigration, Jackson promised to make Georgia a national leader in deportations.

"I don't care if you're Muslim or Mongolian, you don't have the right to force your culture on our country," he said in one ad. "Criminal illegals" who "commit sick, violent crimes" would "end up deported or departed," he promised.

Soon after defeating Jones in a runoff, Jackson shelved the immigration ad, but not before using it as part of a spot featuring his grandchildren. "Granddad, why do you look so mean in these ads?" one asks after watching the "deported or departed" clip on her phone. The children and teenagers then tell their grandfather how he can "look cool" with a pickup truck, a dog and a hipper wardrobe.

"Let's make Georgia better together," the redressed Jackson concludes.

He has since circulated an ad with several young adults who benefited from the millions he spent helping foster children who age out of the Georgia system when they turn 18. "I am so proud of you," he tells them as he chokes up.

On policy, Republican fare and centrist appeals

As he softens his image, Jackson maintains traditional Republican positions, pledging to cut taxes, regulation and what he describes as waste. If he cannot halve the state income tax in four years, he promises not to seek a second term. He wants a balanced budget and full audits of state spending, without saying state law requires a balanced budget and audits of state agencies have long been standard practice.

He says he will expand healthcare without expanding Medicaid under the 2010 Affordable Care Act. Instead, he argues he can fund broader coverage through partnerships with private insurers. That would require Washington to grant permission and commit a level of financial support that no state has gotten without expanding the traditional Medicaid program.

Jackson says he can do all of that while increasing spending on teacher salaries and vocational education.

At the same time, he has toned down his Trump adulation, reflecting Georgia's general election math and voters' frustrations with the Iran war and inflation.

In July, Jackson stood with Trump in Marietta and expressed his hope to "be this guy's favorite governor." When Trump returned to Dalton on Oct. 16, Jackson did not mention Trump at all in his own speech. Later, when the president called him on stage, Jackson praised Trump — for advocating for foster children. When Trump announced that he would be back to Georgia on Saturday, Jackson's campaign initially planned its own event in metro Atlanta before changing it up so Jackson would again be with the president.

Bottoms disputes Jackson's everyman appeal

Bottoms says Jackson is "trying to buy this election" so he can be a Trump stooge. And Democrats have seized on the way that Jackson has talked about the economy.

Discussing trade schools, Jackson said on the debate stage that "my plumber drives a Mercedes." Discussing inflation and crime during his town hall-style debate with Bottoms, he suggested Atlantans felt unsafe "at the gas store" during her tenure. When a citizen in the debate audience asked Jackson about minimum wage and affording basic necessities, Jackson told her, "Hopefully, you're not the one that is getting the $7.50 an hour."

Minimum wage is $7.25. Bottoms has proposed doubling it. Jackson has not proposed any increase. "My focus is creating jobs," he said. "I've been creating jobs my entire life."

Jackson's balancing act is enough for Debbie Satterfield, a 72-year-old who came to a Jackson rally in White County wearing both a Trump shirt and a Jackson sticker.

"When I heard about his harsh upbringing, and to hear how far he had climbed, and starting from nothing," she said. "It reminds me of my life starting with nothing. You can see his soul."

articles.title: Bush dynasty delivers another blow to GOP in Texas Senate battle as family member breaks ranks
articles.summary: Neil Bush revealed he voted for Democrat James Talarico over Ken Paxton, citing deep concerns about Trump's influence on the Republican Party.
articles.body:
Another member of the Bush family dynasty, Neil Bush, is throwing his weight behind Texas Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico, saying he voted against a political style he believes has "damaged our country."

"I have never posted a political message on Facebook, not wanting to offend friends whose views may be very different than mine. I'm breaking that tradition because I voted early today, and I voted for James Talarico for the United States Senate," Neil Bush wrote on Facebook Tuesday.

"My vote was motivated by two things: deep concern about Ken Paxton's record and genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico."

Bush, the son of former President George H.W. Bush and brother of former President George W. Bush, broke with his family's longstanding Republican political tradition in backing the Democrat.

Former President George W. Bush has maintained friendly relationships with Democratic former presidents, but his relationship with President Donald Trump has been strained since the 2016 Republican presidential primary, when Trump repeatedly attacked his brother Jeb Bush and mocked their mother, former first lady Barbara Bush.

"I believe Donald Trump and those who have enabled him have done enormous damage to the Republican Party. I worry about a political culture in which loyalty to an individual takes precedence over loyalty to principle, and where those who hold power begin to believe they are no longer accountable," Neil Bush added.

"But my vote today was about much more than opposition to Ken Paxton."

Neil is the second member of the Bush family to recently throw his support behind Talarico. Barbara Bush, daughter of former President George W. Bush, contributed $2,500 on Sept. 23 to Lone Star Rising PAC, a super PAC supporting the Democrat, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by Fox News Digital.

Lone Star Rising PAC is one of the major outside groups spending to support Talarico and oppose Paxton in the closely contested Texas Senate race, according to federal campaign finance records.

The younger Bush's support for a Democrat comes as his brother, former President George W. Bush, has increasingly embraced bipartisan relationships after his presidency, most recently attending the opening of former President Barack Obama's presidential center in Chicago in June.

Bush and Michelle Obama have repeatedly spoken warmly about their friendship despite their political differences.

At the Obama Center opening , Bush even gave Michelle Obama Altoids, recreating their famous mint/cough-drop exchange from John McCain's 2018 funeral.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House, representatives for Neil Bush and the Paxton campaign for comment.

articles.title: Trump’s former campaign manager on GOP ahead of midterms: ‘It’s ugly’
articles.summary: President Trump’s former campaign manager is joining a growing list predicting midterm doom for Republicans, highlighting recent allegations of government corruption as a key reason. Bill Stepien, who managed Trump’s 2020 campaign and had a stint as White House political director in the president’s first term, told CNN’s Abby Phillip that recent scandals in the…
articles.body:
President Trump’s former campaign manager is joining a growing list predicting midterm doom for Republicans, highlighting recent allegations of government corruption as a key reason.

Bill Stepien, who managed Trump’s 2020 campaign and had a stint as White House political director in the president’s first term, told CNN’s Abby Phillip that recent scandals in the administration — namely the ouster of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle — have contributed to the GOP’s poor showing in most polls.

“We talked a lot about draining the swamp 10 years ago. People wonder what’s changed when they see headlines like Guilfoyle and the trappings and the text messages,” Stepien said. “It’s ugly, and it’s given Democrats an opening.”

Guilfoyle resigned after a series of reports in The Wall Street Journal alleging she asked a GOP donor to help pay her $100,000 credit card bill ahead of her confirmation hearing.

Recent polling shows corruption is a growing issue for Americans heading into the midterms, nearing the importance of cost of living or the economy in some surveys.

Phillip cited a CNBC survey showing 36 percent of registered voters listed government corruption as the most important issue facing the country — higher than the cost of food and groceries.

A Fox News poll found that 90 percent of voters were either extremely or very concerned about government corruption, ahead of those who said the same about inflation and high prices.

The grim mood is contributing to a worsening midterm environment for Republicans, who now trail Democrats on the generic ballot by an average of 7.9 points, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s partner.

The president is attempting to boost his party by making big promises out on the campaign trail. Earlier this fall, he promised $5,000 to every voter if Republicans held control of Congress.

Trump told voters in North Carolina that Camp Lejeune toxic water settlements would be on the way, but only if the GOP wins.

“If we don’t win, there’s no money,” he said at a rally in Greenville, N.C. “If we do win, you’re getting it.”

He also tied disaster relief funds in a handful of states to Republican victories.

Overall, DDHQ’s forecast favors Democrats in the House with a 79 percent chance to flip the chamber, and narrowly favors them in the Senate, with a narrower 57 percent chance of control.

articles.title: Bill Maher fires back at liberal critics over second Trump dinner
articles.summary: Bill Maher fired back at critics during his "Real Time" monologue after attending a second White House dinner with Trump, Stephen A. Smith and Kid Rock.
articles.body: Comedian Bill Maher had a string of harsh words Friday for critics who may have taken issue with his second dinner with President Donald Trump at the White House last week. During his opening monologue on HBO’s "Real Time," Maher hit back against criticism of his latest dinner with Trump — in which sports commentator Stephen A. Smith and musician Kid Rock also attended. "Yeah, I did it again, b----es," Maher said, referring to the Oct. 15 dinner, which followed his first dinner with Trump in April 2025. He then doubled down on his decision to attend, adding, "You know what? F--- you. I like these dinners." BILL MAHER CLAIMS DONALD TRUMP FELT 'BETRAYED' BY HIM WITH 'SILLY' FEUD AFTER CORDIAL 2025 DINNER Maher's confirmation that he attended a second White House dinner comes after Trump told reporters last week that he enjoyed his time eating alongside the three celebrities. "The dinner last night with Kid Rock and Stephen A. [Smith] and Bill Maher was great," Trump said. "I think they had a good time." The president added that Maher "likes me a lot more than people understand." "We talked about everything. It lasted a long time," Trump added. TRUMP SPILLS DETAILS ABOUT DINNER WITH BILL MAHER, STEPHEN A SMITH AND KID ROCK AT THE WHITE HOUSE In the days leading up to the meal, Maher said he would be dining with the president. "I'm having dinner with him again next week," Maher told Hollywood agent and executive Ari Emanuel during a conversation on Maher's "Club Random" podcast earlier this month. "After the first dinner, I went back to doing what I do ... But then, like, he just, out of the blue, let's have dinner again. And I was like, great. And he was really nice," Maher said. "Like, I promise I won't say bad things about you like I did the last time.' And I texted back, and I said, 'You know what, you're the president of the United States. Say whatever the f--- you want. I'm just glad we're talking.' It's like being called a 'hockey puck' by Don Rickles. It's just what he does. It's how he talks." Maher previously made headlines in April 2025 after dining at the White House with Trump, Kid Rock and UFC CEO Dana White. He later told his audience he may have misjudged the president’s demeanor, saying Trump was "more self-aware" in private. "You can hate me for it, but I’m not a liar. Trump was gracious and measured," Maher said in 2025. "And why isn’t that in other settings? I don’t know, and I can’t answer, and it’s not my place to answer. I’m just telling you what I saw, and I wasn’t high." BILL MAHER REVEALS HE'S HAVING DINNER WITH TRUMP AGAIN, SAYS HE WAS 'REALLY NICE' BY TEXT However, Maher has continued to criticize the president. In June, he mocked Trump’s Iran deal, saying the president went from demanding "unconditional surrender" to settling for a memorandum of understanding (MOU) while the White House touted the framework as a foreign policy win. "We got everything we wanted except for everything we asked for," Maher said. Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, told Fox News Digital that he thought Maher’s acknowledgment of his second dinner with Trump was likely the result of a preconceived plan to double-down on his attendance. "Maher walked in with a plan. His Friday monologue showed it. I said last week that each event guest needs a prepared message in anticipation of public criticism," Mudd said. Mudd said Maher's willingness to address criticism directly while appearing genuine could help him retain support from fans who object to his relationship with Trump. "If Bill Maher were my client, I'd advise him to keep sounding like himself. A host who sounds like a surrogate loses credibility," he said. "Maher sounded like Maher, so that risk stays low. Repetition is the next risk, because each new dinner invites the same questions." "Comedians win by joking first, not by clarifying," Mudd added. "Naming the backlash before his critics do takes much of their power away." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News’ Joseph A. Wulfsohn contributed to this report.

articles.title: Obama endorses Nixon, Jolly in last-minute campaign boost
articles.summary: Former President Obama has endorsed the Democratic candidates in Florida’s Senate and gubernatorial races less than two weeks ahead of the midterm elections. Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly and Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon both shared videos of Obama showing support for their campaigns Saturday morning on social platform X. “Real change starts when…
articles.body:
Former President Obama has endorsed the Democratic candidates in Florida’s Senate and gubernatorial races less than two weeks ahead of the midterm elections.

Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly and Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon both shared videos of Obama showing support for their campaigns Saturday morning on social platform X.

“Real change starts when regular folks stand up for what’s right and Angie has spent her career standing up for you,” Obama, who won Florida in both his presidential campaigns, said in a video shared by Nixon in her post .

In the video, Obama said that Nixon has consistently fought for policies to help people including $15 minimum wage and trying to stop congressional redistricting in Florida.

“One leader willing to stand up again and again for what’s right,” he said. “That’s why I believe Angie will be an outstanding U.S. Senator.”

Nixon said in her post that both she and Obama started as organizers in their communities “because we immediately understood that real changes come from regular folks joining the fight.”

Since her win in the Democratic primary earlier this year, Nixon has garnered support from several lawmakers, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who campaigned with her last week, as she takes on her GOP opponent, Sen, Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), who was appointed to Marco Rubio’s seat when he became Secretary of State.

In the video shared by Jolly in his post , Obama called the former Republican congressman turned Democrat “independent-minded” and said he is “focused on lowering the cost of housing and healthcare and making sure every child gets a great education.”

“Elections are about who will fight for you and in this election, it’s David Jolly,” he added. “So, let’s do this Florida. Vote for the change you deserve.”

In his post, Jolly said he is honored to have Obama’s support.

Jolly served one term in the House as a Republican before becoming an independent in 2019. He registered as a Democrat last year and launched his gubernatorial bid. Jolly will face off against Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) in November.

articles.title: Melania Trump's advisor reveals how she bridged Putin, Zelenskyy to broker frontline Ukraine truce
articles.summary: First lady Melania Trump "single-handedly" brokered a humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, Ukraine, her senior advisor says, as Russia extends the truce.
articles.body: First lady Melania Trump helped broker a humanitarian ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine to allow emergency aid into the frontline town of Oleshky, her senior advisor said. Speaking on "Fox & Friends Weekend," exclusive senior advisor Marc Beckman said the agreement followed weeks of mediation involving Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Beckman told Fox News the effort reflects how Trump is redefining the role of first lady. RECOVERING FROM LUNG SURGERY, POPE LEO URGES PUTIN TO AGREE TO CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIAN-HELD UKRAINE CITY "We have to look, as Americans, at our first lady with immense pride. She is completely revamping the role of first lady from somebody building policy awareness into action-oriented. She's saving lives," Beckman said. "Yesterday, she brokered — single-handedly brokered — a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine within the area of Oleshky," he added, noting that Russia has since agreed to extend the planned ceasefire by two days and expand it to a broader area of Ukraine's Kherson region. TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE Beckman said the first lady was moved to negotiate the ceasefire to help elderly residents still trapped in the region, giving them time to evacuate and allowing humanitarian aid to reach those who remain. He said the agreement built on the first lady's previous humanitarian work. Since August 2025, Trump has helped negotiate the release of Ukrainian children from Russia, allowing them to reunite with their families. Beckman said 34 children have been returned to their families through six separate exchanges. KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE "She was smart enough to realize that by leveraging the relationships — the strong relationships that she fostered over six unique moments in time for the reunification of Ukrainian and Russian children... by leveraging those relationships, she was able to bring everybody to the table and negotiate this ceasefire," Beckman said. ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE President Donald Trump also praised his wife's efforts, saying, "I think she's done a great job. I mean, she's into saving babies and bringing babies back home to their parents, and she's been able to do something that's great." Pope Leo XIV reportedly spoke with Putin and Zelenskyy by phone to emphasize the need for a humanitarian truce. UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY OPEN TO FREEZING FRONT LINES IN CEASEFIRE WITH RUSSIA The localized ceasefire is expected to begin Oct. 29, according to the White House. The first lady described the situation in Oleshky as "dire" and said the remaining elderly residents urgently need medical care, medicine, food and drinking water. articles.title: Second Amendment fight moves beyond guns with Supreme Court poised for big ruling
articles.summary: Federal courts extended Second Amendment protections to switchblade knives and body armor, fueling optimism ahead of the Supreme Court's AR-15 case.
articles.body: Two federal court rulings Wednesday extending Second Amendment protections to switchblade knives and body armor have fueled optimism among gun-rights advocates ahead of a major Supreme Court showdown over bans on AR-15-style rifles. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a federal law restricting the interstate commerce of switchblade knives violated the Second Amendment, while a federal judge in the Western District of New York struck down New York’s restrictions on personal body armor. In both cases, the courts determined that switchblades and body armor qualify as constitutionally protected "arms." The twin rulings come as the Supreme Court prepares to hear oral arguments in Viramontes v. Cook County, a case that could determine whether AR-15-style rifles qualify as "arms" protected by the Second Amendment. National Association for Gun Rights President Dudley Brown, whose organization filed an amicus brief in Viramontes, said a Supreme Court ruling against AR-15 bans could influence future legal challenges to restrictions on ammunition magazines, automatic knives, body armor and other defensive equipment. "The interesting thing about both of these cases is that they’re both going to be really decided by the U.S. Supreme Court in the Viramontes decision," Brown told Fox News Digital. SUPREME COURT UNANIMOUSLY LIMITS USE OF GUN LAW USED TO PROSECUTE HUNTER BIDEN The recent rulings rely on two major Supreme Court decisions defining the scope of the Second Amendment: District of Columbia v. Heller and New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen — both of which will play a key role in the Supreme Court’s review of AR-15-style rifle bans. In its 2008 decision in Heller, the Supreme Court established that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess firearms for lawful purposes, including self-defense. The Court also ruled that the amendment protects weapons in lawful common use while acknowledging a longstanding tradition of restricting "dangerous and unusual" weapons. Heller recognized that the term "arms" encompasses both offensive weapons and defensive armor. The decision did not address switchblades or body armor directly but the recent rulings relied on its broader understanding of what may qualify as an arm. The decisions also reveal how Bruen ’s text-and-history test could shape the Supreme Court’s review of bans on AR-15-style rifles. Under Bruen, courts first determine whether the Second Amendment’s text covers the weapon or conduct at issue. Because both courts answered that question affirmatively, the burden shifted to the governments to show that the restrictions were consistent with the nation’s historical tradition of arms regulation. George Lyon, a Second Amendment attorney, said the governments in both cases failed to identify sufficiently similar historical laws justifying the modern restrictions. ATF SUSPENDS FEDERAL REGISTRATION AND APPROVAL RULES FOR CERTAIN FIREARMS "Once what you want to do is shown to come within the text of the Second Amendment, the presumption is that the regulation is unconstitutional," Lyon said. The Fifth Circuit found that switchblades are commonly used "arms" protected by the Second Amendment, citing their historical use for defense and everyday purposes. It then ruled that the government had failed to identify a sufficient historical tradition for the Federal Switchblade Act’s specific restrictions on interstate commerce, which regulated switchblades in a way that differed from historical laws. In the New York ruling, the state argued that body armor was a tactical accessory to a firearm rather than an "arm" protected by the Second Amendment. The judge rejected that argument, finding that body armor falls within the historical definition of arms recognized in Heller. The court then concluded that New York had not shown a sufficient historical tradition supporting its civilian purchase ban. That reasoning could become important in Viramontes, where the Supreme Court is being asked to decide whether AR-15-style rifles fall within the definition of protected arms recognized in Heller. GUN RIGHTS GROUPS CAPITALIZE AFTER JUDGE REVERSES DECADES-OLD RESTRICTIONS: 'MONUMENTAL' The case arises from a challenge to Cook County’s assault-weapons ban. The Seventh Circuit concluded that AR-15-style rifles were comparable to machine guns and therefore fell outside the category of arms protected by the Second Amendment. The Supreme Court’s decision could resolve whether that reasoning is consistent with Heller and Bruen. Lyon said the Seventh Circuit improperly treated AR-15-style rifles as comparable to machine guns. "The current case at the Supreme Court, Viramontes, will address that because the Seventh Circuit had taken the position that because AR-15s are ‘like machine guns,’ they don’t constitute an arm as defined under Heller," Lyon said. "That was just totally wrong in my view." Justin Davis, director of public affairs for the National Rifle Association, said the dispute over AR-15-style rifles is part of a broader legal fight over what qualifies as an "arm" under the Second Amendment. "There’s a major discussion going on in the courts about what is and what aren’t arms," Davis said. Davis pointed to litigation involving suppressors, ammunition magazines, stun guns, pepper spray and other equipment used for self-defense. "They talk about how the Second Amendment only applied to muskets because that’s what existed at the time of the Founders, but we don’t apply the First Amendment only to newspapers, books or speech in public forums," Davis said. "Social media, texting and phones didn’t exist at that time, either." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The world evolves, but the core fundamental rights never change," Davis continued.

articles.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump’s DOJ keeps close eye on election results; Last-minute campaigning heats up
articles.summary: With less than two weeks to go before the midterms, the Trump administration is ramping up its warnings about voter fraud and is not ruling out the prospect of weighing in on states’ election certification efforts. The Justice Department (DOJ) reportedly sent letters Friday to California election officials, directing them to identify potential noncitizens on…
articles.body:
With less than two weeks to go before the midterms, the Trump administration is ramping up its warnings about voter fraud and is not ruling out the prospect of weighing in on states’ election certification efforts.

The Justice Department (DOJ) reportedly sent letters Friday to California election officials, directing them to identify potential noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls or “risk significant federal scrutiny.”

This move followed the DOJ’s lawsuit filed last week against California after state and local officials refused to cross-reference 20,000 names on its voter rolls with a list of individuals the Department of Homeland Security flagged over citizenship status concerns.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) accused President Trump at a campaign event in New Hampshire on Sunday of “trying to quite literally rig the election.”

“He’s trying to get our voting rolls,” he said. “You can’t make this stuff up.”

On Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche did not rule out intervening in states’ midterm election certification processes, citing the need to do so in a potential “doomsday scenario” when reporters asked him about the matter.

The attorney general added the DOJ has no intention “to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.”

A day later, the DOJ sued to block Alaska from verifying its election results, arguing the fact two candidates in the state’s Senate race share the same name could taint the results. Democrats were quick to slam this move as an attempt from the Trump administration to control the outcome of the competition between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D).

Blanche will join CBS News’s “Face the Nation” and CNN “State of the Union” Sunday, while California Sen. Adam Schiff (D) will appear on NBC News’s “Meet the Press.”

Decision Desk HQ, a nonpartisan election handicapper, gives Democrats an 80 percent chance of retaking control of the House this November as of Saturday. But it predicts a tighter fight for the Senate, with DDHQ giving the party having a 56 percent likelihood of gaining the majority in the upper chamber.

Democrats are already putting plans in place for their anticipated takeover of Congress and weighing how they would confront the Trump administration if given back the majority.

Trump told reporters Friday he would “veto everything” if the Democrats regained control of the legislature.

“You veto, veto, veto, and then they come and they say, ‘How do we get it done?’ And you make a deal,” the president said.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who has signaled he would not step down from leading Republicans in the lower chamber should his party lose its majority, will appear on Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday.”

Several candidates running in closely watched battleground midterm races are also expected to make an appearance on Sunday broadcasts.

Iowa Senate candidates Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) will both appear on ABC News’s “This Week” on Sunday. GOP Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers will join “Meet the Press,” while Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D), will appear on “Face the Nation.”

Though Ohio’s gubernatorial candidates are not slated to appear on any Sunday talk shows, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial campaign ad featuring Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s mother may also pop up as a topic of conversation on these broadcasts — as the commercial sparked a media firestorm throughout the week.

DDHQ lists the race between Ramaswamy and Acton as leaning in the Democrat’s favor by around four points. The Ohio Senate race places former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, around the same distance ahead of Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted.

Fuel shortages brought on by the ongoing Iran war continue to strain global energy supplies and ramp up pressure on the Trump administration to address rising costs at the pump ahead of the midterm elections.

On Thursday, the president signed an executive order aimed at lowering mortgage payments amid rising borrowing costs .

The order directs the Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte to form a pilot program to cancel insurance premiums for government-backed mortgages once a borrower meets certain requirements. It also establishes a task force to lower home construction costs .

Additionally, the White House announced Friday it was lifting tariffs on certain Canadian goods after these economic policies faced bipartisan criticism ahead of Nov. 3.

The New York Times reported Wednesday American and Israeli militaries had developed plans for strikes after the midterm elections. The two countries launched initial strikes in this conflict on Feb. 28. Meanwhile, a Friday U.S. intelligence memo signaled Iranian plots to attack and kill Americans abroad had reached “advanced stages.”

In other international news, Ukrainian officials announced Saturday Starshield satellite services were back up to normal speeds in the country after a controversial slowdown, reportedly ordered by billionaire tech mogul Elon Musk, impacted their defense systems against Russia.

In a statement shared on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked “all Americans” and partners, such as Congress, the State Department and Trump.

“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky said. “The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient. This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered ‘shaheds.’”

Earlier this week, Russia indicated it was open to resuming trilateral negotiations with Kyiv and Washington. The White House also announced Friday first lady Melania Trump had secured a localized ceasefire deal in a city on the Russia-Ukraine border.

Fox News’s senior strategic analyst, retired Gen. Jack Keane, will appear on the network’s “Sunday Morning Futures.”

articles.title: Obama describes Trump as an agent of ‘chaos and cruelty’ in midterm elections pitch
articles.summary: Former President Barack Obama characterized President Donald Trump as an agent of “chaos and cruelty” and a man of broken promises during a midterm election rally.
articles.body: CLEVELAND — Former President Barack Obama, appearing here Saturday at his first campaign rally for this fall’s midterm elections, characterized President Donald Trump as an agent of “chaos and cruelty” and a man of broken promises. And in a particularly pointed criticism of his Republican successor, Obama mocked Trump’s ballroom construction and the gold accents he has added throughout the White House. “Does anybody really think this guy in the White House right now is spending all that time thinking about these issues?” Obama wondered. “I mean, I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV.” Obama added a moment later: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” The crowd inside a near-capacity Public Auditorium, which holds more than 10,000, erupted with laughter at that and other quips Obama offered throughout his afternoon address. The former president’s visit was aimed at boosting two Democrats: Amy Acton, the party’s nominee for governor, and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who has mounted a comeback bid for his old job. Ohio, which has become more reliably Republican since Trump’s rise in politics, has emerged as an intense battleground this year. Polls show both races are toss-ups, with Democrats especially hopeful of winning the governorship for the first time in 20 years. “This midterm election victory runs through Ohio,” Rep. Shontel Brown, a Democrat whose district includes a large part of Cleveland, said as she warmed up the crowd. Trump has rallied in the state twice in recent weeks, with a pitch primarily focused on Brown’s Republican rival, Sen. Jon Husted. Trump will return next week for an event in Chillicothe, a smaller, working-class city that served as Ohio’s first state capital. Meanwhile, the race for governor was jolted this week by the decision by Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, to air an explosive attack ad that features Acton’s estranged mother calling her a “liar.” The ad was met with swift and bipartisan condemnation for drawing on a family’s painful history of alleged sexual abuse. Obama was particularly scornful of the attack in his speech Saturday. “We all know that guy — who is, like, thirsty,” Obama said of Ramaswamy. “Just wants to get attention no matter what, willing to do anything. And in recent days we’ve seen there is no line he won’t cross.” He added: “I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.” Acton also briefly touched on the controversy in her remarks at the rally, thanking supporters for “the love you have shown” in recent days. “My opponent,” she said, referring to Ramaswamy, “has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his struggling campaign, but it’s not going to work.” In the Ramaswamy campaign’s ad, Donna Arthur calls her daughter a liar and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. Acton has said she has not seen or talked to Arthur in nearly 50 years. Over the years and throughout her campaign, Acton has also talked about having been sexually abused by Arthur’s then-husband as a child. She has said she was removed from Arthur’s custody in 1978, after her then-stepfather was charged with rape. Ramaswamy has defended the ad, and his campaign on Thursday told NBC News that it planned a $4 million push to air it. Trump has expressed his approval, as well. Obama also had kind words for Brown, whom he playfully described as frugal. “He still is wearing the same suit he was in when I met him 20 years ago,” Obama said of Brown, who has a reputation for keeping a rumpled appearance. “You know he got a haircut for this rally, but you all know he’s too cheap to get a haircut more than once every couple months.” Brown, Obama added, “is not somebody pretending to look out for working folks. He has always been there for you, even when it’s hard, even when he might lose an election.” Brown, who spent nearly 50 years in public office before losing his Senate seat in 2024, argued in his speech that “corruption is woven into everything” in Washington. “Politicians who are supposed to be working for you are cashing in,” Brown said. “When they’re in office they play the stock market, and when they leave they become lobbyists.” When Brown linked Husted with billionaires like Elon Musk and Trump, the crowds burst out into chants of “Lock him up!” The moment called back to the “Lock her up!” chants that rang out at Trump rallies when he campaigned against Hillary Clinton in 2016. Meanwhile, Obama’s appearance alongside the Democrats drew rejoinders from their Republican opponents. “Ohioans can’t afford a liberal governor who shows up for Obama but never shows up for them,” said Ramaswamy spokesperson Connie Luck. “The sight of Sherrod Brown and Barack Obama together again should send shivers down Ohioans’ spines,” Amy Natoce, a spokesperson for Husted, said. “The Brown-Obama duo gave us higher taxes, less jobs and wide open borders.” Obama kept much of his 35-minute speech focused on Trump. “Now, two years ago, there were a lot of people who weren’t crazy about the guy’s character, but they were frustrated about post-Covid inflation,” Obama said. “They were seeing prices go up, and they heard him make a bunch of promises to get costs under control.” While Trump has urged voters in this year’s midterm elections to act as if he is on the ballot, Obama suggested they should evaluate Republican candidates by considering whether Trump has lived up to his promises of 2024. He specifically singled out for criticism Trump’s tariffs and the war with Iran, both of which have driven up prices. “In this case, this administration’s actions are directly responsible for rising costs,” Obama said. “The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions. Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for, nobody voted for.” Obama is scheduled to campaign later Saturday in Michigan with Jocelyn Benson and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidates for governor and Senate there. He is focusing this fall on races where he believes he can motivate Democrats and persuadable voters, with an emphasis on closely watched contests like those in Ohio and Michigan, according to his office. Next week, Obama is scheduled to visit Atlanta, where he will campaign alongside Sen. Jon Ossoff and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic candidate for governor in Georgia. The former president — through events, emails and mailings coordinated by Democratic committees — also has helped raise more than $15 million for midterm races, his office said. He has recorded more than two dozen TV and radio spots, and more are expected before Election Day. In his speech here, Obama described the election as a potential “inflection point” and “course correction.” “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in modern times,” Obama said, “you get the chance to say, ‘Enough’s enough. We are going to change right here in Ohio.’”

articles.title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: "This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama said.
articles.body:
Former President Barack Obama attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead the US midterm elections.

On Saturday, the Democrat held a campaign rally in Ohio to stump for candidates Amy Acton and Sherrod Brown. Later, he will appear in Michigan to push for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

Meanwhile, Donald Trump cast his early ballot in Florida, and later on Saturday will head to Georgia to hold a rally for Republican candidates.

Earlier voting has begun ahead of the 3 November elections, which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency.

Speaking on Saturday in Cleveland, Ohio, Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members, and attacked the president for not lowering costs for American consumers while waging war against Iran.

"This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama said.

"This is a circuit breaker in the system. We need to flip that circuit breaker. We need to start bringing some accountability to this administration," the former president said.

Who will win the midterms? How the US elections will be won and lost

What are the US midterms? A simple guide

He said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic.

But he said Trump has only himself to blame for the current state of the economy.

"If you thought everyone was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump, "everything is more expensive now".

He also said that the war has given Iran "veto power" over the Strait of Hormuz, which was open to marine traffic before hostilities began in February.

When asked about the Iran war on Saturday afternoon, Trump said: "I've done it very effectively and I may have to finish it off, or maybe they'll make a deal, but I'm not sure. Either way, we win."

He and and First Lady Melania Trump were casting advance votes in Florida before leaving to Georgia.

Trump also told reporters "we will see" when asked if Melania Trump would visit Ukraine, after the White House said that she "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower oil prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

He recently struck a deal with Russia to export the country's diesel to the US, despite pushback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers.

At his afternoon rally, Obama also took a swipe at Trump's efforts to renovate the White House.

"What's with all the gold? He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory," Obama joked.

Obama's trip to Ohio was to show support for ex-Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running to unseat incumbent Republican Senator John Husted, and Amy Acton, who is running for state governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.

In his remarks, Obama criticised Ramaswamy for a campaign ad released this week in which Acton's estranged mother was featured calling her a liar. The ad didn't mention that the woman's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.

"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross. No low he will not sink to to try to get in the limelight," Obama said. "I mean, think about this latest ad he ran."

Acton also spoke at the campaign rally before Obama to argue that Ramaswamy "has chosen to exploit my childhood" to "save his struggling campaign".

articles.title: Obama on Trump White House: ‘Like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory’
articles.summary: President Obama delivered a harsh assessment Saturday of President Trump’s many Washington renovation projects while rallying supporters for Ohio Democratic midterm candidates former Sen. Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton. “He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of Trump’s over $900 million worth of White House construction efforts. “What’s…
articles.body:
President Obama delivered a harsh assessment Saturday of President Trump’s many Washington renovation projects while rallying supporters for Ohio Democratic midterm candidates former Sen. Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton.

“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of Trump’s over $900 million worth of White House construction efforts. “What’s with the gold? … He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Obama went on to say he believes Trump is more focused on renovating the White House than on the issues voters care about.

But the former president’s attacks did not stop with the White House. Obama went on to blast Trump’s policies and cabinet officials while also taking shots at Republican candidates in his Cleveland speech — full of quips and punchlines.

The Democrat singled out Trump’s original 2016 message to “drain the swamp,” a call to shake up the Washington establishment, jokingly drawing comparisons between the adage and his attempted renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

After the White House unveiled the newly renovated pool in June, onlookers began to spot a growth of green algae in the water and the peeling of newly installed “American flag blue” base paint. After months of renovations and a heated legal battle surrounding vandalism allegations, Trump said Friday the pool is 85 percent done with the refilling process.

“Remember that whole thing about drain the swamp? The only thing that got drained was the Reflecting Pool in the National Mall after some no-bid contract got it all messed up,” Obama said.

The former president also threw out an insult at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a frequent target of Democrats over his handling of the Iran war and his “warriors” not “weirdos” rhetoric. Hegseth has called the military “low-T” and mandated testosterone screenings for male service members under 30.

“You’ve got the defense secretary … he’s very focused on important matters like the jawlines and testosterone levels of our troops,” Obama said. “How much time do you think this defense secretary spends looking at himself in the mirror in the morning?”

And, as cost of living remains a major concern for voters, Obama moved on to criticize Trump’s tariff agenda — specifically his trade war with Canada.

“The big trade war he’s started now is with that well-known evil empire, Canada,” Obama said. “I mean these are the people who gave us maple syrup and Martin Short.”

Obama was the last Democrat running for president to win Ohio, and the party has not fared well in the Buckeye State since. The last time a Democrat other than Brown won a Senate race in Ohio was 1992, a fact which would remain true even if he returns to the Senate come November. The state has not elected a Democratic governor since 2006.

A Bowling Green State University poll released last week found Obama was the only public official to have a positive favorability rating among Ohio voters.

The former president touched on the scandals surrounding some of Ohio’s races — directly addressed Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial attack ad featuring his opponent Acton’s estranged mother, his opponent. Trump and Vice President Vance were among those who defended the commercial despite widespread bipartisan backlash.

“There’s a decency that we should expect out of our public officials. And I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody could run an ad like that,” Obama said of the ad. “No office is worth stooping that low.”

The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment on Obama’s remarks.

articles.title: Obama slams Ramaswamy and Trump in his first rally of the midterms
articles.summary: The former president is again stepping off the sidelines in the closing stretch of an election.
articles.body:
In his first rally of the 2026 midterm cycle, former President Barack Obama slammed President Donald Trump and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, calling out the latter's much-maligned campaign ad centering on Democrat Amy Acton's mother.

"There's gotta be something inside you where you just say no office is worth stooping that low," Obama said of Ramaswamy's choice to run the ad.

With the midterms just over a week away, Obama was rallying in Cleveland in support of Acton and Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown.

Trump, Obama said, had broken a slew of promises he made on the campaign trail in 2024, ensnaring the country in an ongoing war in Iran and failing to bring down costs. Instead, "he's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," the former president said, taking aim at Trump's renovations to the executive mansion.

"We got two more years of this administration," he said. "That's how our system of government works. But you know what we're not stuck with? We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are enabling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people."

Long one of Democrats' top surrogates , Obama is again stepping off the sidelines in the closing stretch of an election. He'll appear in Detroit alongside Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson on Sunday, after which he'll travel to Georgia for a rally with Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms on Oct. 28.

The former president, who captured Ohio's electoral votes in 2008 and 2012, also called out Ramaswamy for his controversial campaign ad featuring Acton's mother . Acton was removed from her mother's home after her stepfather was charged with raping her. She spoke about her childhood in a speech moments before the former president took to the stage on Saturday.

"There's a decency that we should expect out of our public officials," Obama said. "And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody could run an ad like that."

The White House and Ramaswamy's campaign both did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Blanche: DOJ lawsuit not trying to ‘stop the certification of Alaska’s election’
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche said Saturday that the Justice Department is not trying to stop the certification of Alaska’s election, referring to a lawsuit filed this week which claimed to “protect the integrity” of the election. The lawsuit, filed Thursday in the U.S. District Court for the district of Alaska, claims that the inclusion of a candidate…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche said Saturday that the Justice Department is not trying to stop the certification of Alaska’s election, referring to a lawsuit filed this week which claimed to “protect the integrity” of the election.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday in the U.S. District Court for the district of Alaska, claims that the inclusion of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) could give Democrat Mary Peltola an unfair advantage in the upcoming Senate election.

The lawsuit filing said Daniel J. Sullivan entered the Senate race “as a Republican with the intention of misleading” the incumbent senator’s supporters, and that the sole purpose of his candidacy is “to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan.”

“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” the filing reads.

“The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” it added.

Blanche, in a post on social platform X , said the lawsuit, which President Trump has said he directed to be filed, “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.”

“This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead,” he added.

In an interview with MS Now, Peltola called the Justice Department’s lawsuit “a very desperate attempt to cling to power.”

“We’ve been running great elections for decades. There have never really been any abnormalities or irregularities to speak of,” the Democratic Senate nominee said. “I have total confidence in Alaskans’ ability to know who they’re voting for.”

Earlier this year, Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign faced legal challenges with the director of the Alaska Division of Elections, Carol Beecher, trying to remove him from the primary ballot and disqualify his campaign, citing his logo’s similarities to Sen. Sullivan’s.

The Petersburg resident with no party affiliation , challenged the measure in court, leading to a Superior Court judge’s ruling in June that allowed him to stay on the ballot for the state’s primary in August.

articles.title: Obama compares Trump's White House renovations to 'Saddam Hussein opening a Cheesecake Factory' at Ohio rally
articles.summary: Barack Obama compared Trump's White House renovations to a Cheesecake Factory run by Saddam Hussein at a Cleveland rally for Ohio Democrats.
articles.body: Former President Barack Obama mocked President Donald Trump's White House renovations Saturday, comparing the historic residence to a Cheesecake Factory run by Saddam Hussein while campaigning for Democrats in Ohio. Obama delivered the jab during a Cleveland rally supporting Democrat gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, criticizing Trump's priorities just 10 days before the midterm elections. "I mean, I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovations," Obama said. "He should be on HGTV." OBAMA CLAIMS HE OCCUPIES 'A SUITE' IN TRUMP'S MIND, QUESTIONS THE PRESIDENT'S FOCUS ON AMERICANS Obama rattled off Trump's ballroom project, Rose Garden makeover and South Lawn helipad before taking aim at the president's affinity for gold décor. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama quipped. The renovations, however, include several functional upgrades to the White House grounds. TRUMP DEFENDS US INTERVENTIONS ABROAD AHEAD OF 'BIG DECISION' ON IRAN: 'SETTLING YEARS OF UNFINISHED BUSINESS' The Rose Garden's former central lawn was replaced with limestone paving in 2025, creating a patio for outdoor events, speeches and entertaining, while the traditional roses were retained around the perimeter. Trump also unveiled an upgraded granite White House helipad featuring the presidential seal in September. Official White House photographs show Marine One landing on and departing from the new facility during a Sept. 21 ribbon-cutting ceremony. The administration's ballroom project is intended to provide permanent, secure space for large official events, addressing a longstanding reliance on temporary tents for major White House functions. A National Park Service environmental assessment notes that the need for expanded event space was identified in a White House planning document dating to 2000. Obama's swipe at Trump's White House makeover comes as his own presidential center in Chicago has faced criticism over its imposing, granite-clad tower, which some critics have dubbed the 'Obamalisk,' along with ballooning construction costs and years of delays. The Obama Presidential Center's projected price tag has surpassed $1 billion, nearly triple its original $350 million estimate, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting. Subcontractors have alleged they are owed millions for their work, while taxpayers have been saddled with hundreds of millions of dollars in associated public infrastructure costs separate from the center's construction budget. Obama's criticism extended beyond the presidential residence to Trump's handling of the conflict with Iran, which the former president blamed for higher energy costs. "Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for and nobody voted for," Obama said. He also defended the nuclear agreement negotiated during his presidency. TRUMP RIPS OBAMA'S 'STUPID' IRAN DEAL, CLAIMS FORMER PRESIDENT THOUGHT 'HE COULD BRIBE THEM' "Iran didn't have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place that everybody knows kept them from getting nukes," Obama claimed. Trump withdrew the United States from the 2015 agreement in 2018, arguing that its temporary nuclear restrictions were insufficient and that it failed to adequately address Iran's ballistic missile program and support for regional militant terror groups. The agreement offered Tehran sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear restrictions and international inspections. Inspectors reported some Iranian compliance before the U.S. withdrawal, although Iran subsequently expanded uranium enrichment beyond the deal's proposed limits. Obama also accused Trump of pursuing policies that increased consumer costs, criticizing immigration enforcement as he urged Ohio voters to hold Republicans accountable. Acton faces Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the governor's race, while Brown is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted. The former president carried Ohio in both 2008 and 2012, but the state has backed Trump in his three presidential campaigns. The former president’s speech went after several Republican figures and recent scandals, often jokingly, as…
articles.body:
President Obama took aim at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for his perceived focus on soldiers’ appearances and testosterone levels during a campaign stop in Cleveland, Ohio on Saturday while campaign for gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown.

The former president’s speech went after several Republican figures and recent scandals, often jokingly, as he made the case for Ohioans to support Acton and Brown, following years of rightward swings in the Buckeye State. Obama was the last Democratic nominee to win Ohio, doing so in both his campaigns in 2008 and 2012.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has been a frequent target of Democrats over his handling of the Iran war and his “warriors” not “weirdos” rhetoric. Hegseth has called the military “low-T” and mandated testosterone screenings for male service members under 30.

“You’ve got the defense secretary … he’s very focused on important matters like the jawlines and testosterone levels of our troops,” Obama said.

The former president made the case that Hegseth’s focus on these issues has been a distraction and contributed to the prolonged Iran conflict.

Obama went further, adding “How much time do you think this defense secretary spends looking at himself in the mirror in the morning?”

The 44th president’s comments come as Senate Democrats are quietly floating the ouster of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth after the Nov. 3 election as the political price for cooperation on key defense-related issues in the postelection lame-duck session, and they may have some GOP support to shake up the Pentagon’s leadership, according to Senate sources.

articles.title: Quais os documentos que precisa para votar no segundo turno? | G1
articles.standfirst: Eleitor precisa apenas de um documento oficial com foto, mas deve saber qual zona e seção eleitoral em que vota; informações podem ser consultadas on-line no site do TSE.
articles.summary: Eleitor precisa apenas de um documento oficial com foto, mas deve saber qual zona e seção eleitoral em que vota; informações podem ser consultadas on-line no site do TSE.
articles.body:
Para votar, o eleitor precisa apenas de um documento oficial com foto, mas precisa saber qual sua zona e seção eleitoral. — Foto: Érico Andrade/G1

Para votar no segundo turno das eleições de 2026 , o eleitor deve apresentar um documento oficial com foto aos mesários . O título de eleitor em papel não é obrigatório e, na maioria dos casos, nem precisa ser levado.

Também é possível votar usando apenas o aplicativo e-Título , desde que ele exiba a fotografia do eleitor. Caso a versão digital não tenha foto, será necessário apresentar outro documento oficial com foto.

Quais documentos são aceitos para votar?

A Justiça Eleitoral aceita os seguintes documentos oficiais com foto para identificar o eleitor no dia da votação:

carteira de categoria profissional reconhecida por lei , como OAB, CRM, CREA e outros conselhos profissionais.

Mesmo que estejam vencidos, esses documentos podem ser aceitos, desde que permitam identificar o eleitor.

Já a certidão de nascimento e a certidão de casamento não são válidas para votar , pois não possuem fotografia.

É obrigatório levar o título de eleitor?

Não. O título de eleitor em papel não é exigido para votar. O documento serve apenas para facilitar a consulta da zona eleitoral e da seção onde o eleitor vota.

Se o eleitor souber o local de votação, basta apresentar um documento oficial com foto . Nem mesmo o e-Título é obrigatório, caso o eleitor saiba sua zona e seção eleitoral.

Sim, desde que a versão do aplicativo exiba a foto do eleitor. Nessa situação, o e-Título pode ser utilizado sozinho para a identificação na seção eleitoral, sem necessidade de apresentar outro documento.

Se o aplicativo não mostrar a fotografia — normalmente porque o eleitor ainda não fez o cadastro biométrico — será obrigatório apresentar também um documento oficial com foto (lista acima).

Quem vota no exterior precisa dos mesmos documentos. Brasileiros inscritos para votar no exterior também podem utilizar o e-Título. Da mesma forma, quando o aplicativo não exibe a fotografia, o eleitor deverá apresentar um documento oficial com foto para comprovar sua identidade.

Para evitar problemas na hora de votar, a recomendação é levar um dos documentos com fotos listados acima .

Caso não tenha o e-Título ou a versão impressa em mãos, o ideal é ir para o local de votação sabendo qual a zona e a seção eleitoral, que podem ser consultados no site do TSE ou nos portais dos tribunais regionais.

articles.title: Qual a diferença entre o voto branco e nulo? Entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Série especial do g1 com 50 vídeos explica os principais temas das eleições de 2026.
articles.summary: Série especial do g1 com 50 vídeos explica os principais temas das eleições de 2026.
articles.body:
Neste domingo (25), dia do segundo turno das Eleições 2026 , os brasileiros voltam às urnas para escolher o próximo presidente da República . Voto branco e voto nulo são registrados de maneiras diferentes na urna eletrônica, mas têm o mesmo efeito na apuração: ambos são desconsiderados na contagem dos votos válidos e não são destinados a nenhum candidato ou partido.

A principal diferença está na maneira como o eleitor escolhe não votar em uma candidatura.

Antes da adoção das urnas eletrônicas, a votação era feita em cédulas de papel. O voto em branco acontecia quando o eleitor deixava a cédula sem marcar nenhuma opção.

Com a urna eletrônica, o papel em branco foi substituído pelo botão branco. Para votar em branco, basta apertar a tecla correspondente e, em seguida, a tecla verde, de confirmação.

O voto nulo ocorre quando o eleitor digita na urna um número que não corresponde a nenhum candidato ou partido e confirma a escolha.

Na época das cédulas de papel, era possível anular o voto escrevendo um nome que não correspondesse a nenhum candidato. A prática chegou a render alguns episódios curiosos da história eleitoral brasileira.

Nos anos 1950, por exemplo, o rinoceronte Cacareco recebeu cerca de 100 mil votos em São Paulo. Na década de 1980, no Rio de Janeiro, foi a vez do macaco Tião ganhar notoriedade nas urnas.

Apesar da votação expressiva, nenhum dos dois assumiu cargo político. Os votos foram considerados nulos e, portanto, não foram contabilizados para o resultado da eleição.

Urna eletrônica eleições mulher — Foto: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral/TSE

Votos brancos e nulos contam para o resultado da eleição?

Para definir o resultado da eleição, a Justiça Eleitoral considera apenas os votos válidos — aqueles dados a candidatos ou partidos devidamente registrados para aquela disputa.

Assim, se um eleitor vota em branco ou anula o voto, essa escolha não é contabilizada para nenhum candidato.

Embora não alterem a definição de quem será eleito, os votos brancos e nulos ajudam a mostrar como parte do eleitorado se comportou naquela eleição.

Neste domingo (25), quando Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) disputam o segundo turno das Eleições 2026 , assim que a votação for encerrada, às 17h (horário de Brasília), e os primeiros dados começarem a ser divulgados, o eleitor poderá acompanhar ao vivo a apuração dos votos pelo g1 :

Os dados são do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) .

Na página de apuração do g1 , o usuário pode acessar os números de votos em cada unidade federativa em tempo real e acompanhar a apuração.

Além das páginas de apuração, o g1 terá uma série de recursos especiais para facilitar o acompanhamento das Eleições 2026. Resultados em tempo real, vídeo ao vivo, mapas interativos e conteúdos automatizados estarão disponíveis nas homes e em páginas especiais do portal (veja abaixo).

Apuração das Eleições 2026: acompanhe os resultados em tempo real

Além da apuração nacional, acesse diretamente as páginas com os resultados do segundo turno nos cinco estados e no Distrito Federal:

O que você encontra na página de apuração

Ao acessar o estado desejado, você encontrará um resumo da corrida eleitoral da região, começando pela lista dos candidatos . Também é possível acessar o resumo da corrida presidencial.

Até as 17h de domingo (25), os candidatos estarão listados por ordem alfabética. Conforme os dados da apuração forem liberados pelo TSE, os nomes serão listados de acordo com a quantidade de votos recebidos.

Em seguida, um gráfico mostrará, do início ao fim da apuração, a evolução dos candidatos mais bem colocados ( imagem abaixo ).

Será possível navegar pelos mapas interativos do Brasil e dos estados para ver os resultados da eleição para presidente nos 5.571 municípios.

A consulta será detalhada em todas as cidades : o eleitor poderá fazer a busca na lupa ( no canto superior direito do mapa ) e conferir os votos por zona eleitoral, local de votação e urna. Só clicar em "Ver zonas eleitorais" (veja na imagem abaixo) .
