articles.summary: Pelo menos 8 estados terão proibição de venda de bebida alcoólica no segundo turno das Eleições, que acontece neste domingo (25).
articles.body:
Pelo menos 8 estados terão proibição de venda de bebida alcoólica no segundo turno das Eleições 2026 , que acontece neste domingo (25). A restrição, que antes tinha alcance nacional, passou a ser segmentada por estados e decidida pelos tribunais regionais.

➡️ Os estados que terão a proibição são: Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Maranhão, Mato Grosso, Pará, Piauí e Roraima.

➡️ Enquanto isso, 15 unidades da federação não terão restrição: Alagoas, Ceará, Distrito Federal, Espírito Santo, Goiás, Mato Grosso do Sul, Minas Gerais, Paraíba, Paraná, Pernambuco, Rio de Janeiro, Rio Grande do Norte, Rio Grande do Sul e Sergipe.

➡️ Também há estados em que a decisão é local e deve ser feita por zonas eleitorais, ficando a cargo dos juízes eleitorais destas regiões. São eles: Bahia. Ainda não há informações sobre Santa Catarina, São Paulo, Rondônia.

🔎 A lei foi criada para evitar situações de desordem nos locais de votação ou nas proximidades a partir do consumo de bebida alcoólica.

Portaria do TRE-AC proíbe a venda de bebidas alcoólicas nas Eleições no estado — Foto: Érico Andrade/g1

Veja abaixo em quais estados haverá ou não proibição da venda de bebidas alcoólicas.

A venda e o consumo de bebidas alcoólicas estarão proibidos em todo o Acre da 0h às 16h do domingo (25), dia do segundo turno das Eleições 2026. A medida vale para estabelecimentos comerciais, serviços de entrega e locais públicos.

Segundo a portaria do Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Acre (TRE-AC), a restrição inclui a venda, a distribuição e o fornecimento de bebidas alcoólicas, mesmo de forma gratuita. O descumprimento da determinação poderá configurar crime de desobediência, previsto no Código Eleitoral.

A Secretaria de Segurança Pública de Alagoas (SSP-AL) informou que não haverá proibição à comercialização de bebidas alcoólicas em hotéis, bares, restaurantes e por vendedores ambulantes durante o segundo turno das Eleições 2026 no estado.

Na prática, isso garante a liberação de venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Amapá (TRE-AP) confirmou a proibição da venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante as Eleições 2026. O tribunal ainda não indicou a faixa de horário em que as restrições acontecerão.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Amazonas (TRE-AM) e a Secretaria de Segurança Pública do Amazonas (SSP-AM) proibiram o consumo de bebidas alcoólicas em estabelecimentos e locais abertos ao público durante o dia da eleição. A restrição vale em todo o estado das 2h às 17h de domingo (25).

A proibição vale para bares, restaurantes, supermercados, mercearias e estabelecimentos similares, além de outros locais abertos ao público. O descumprimento da determinação será considerado crime de desobediência, previsto no artigo 347 do Código Eleitoral (Lei nº 4.737/1965).

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral da Bahia (TRE-BA) informou que a regra será discricionária , então cada zona eleitoral pode decretar ou não. Mais de 200 cidades no estado terão restrições ou proibições para a venda e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no segundo turno das eleições.

Salvador não aparece na lista divulgada pelo TRE-BA e, até a última atualização desta reportagem, nenhuma zona eleitoral da capital havia determinado a Lei Seca.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Ceará NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Distrito Federal NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Espírito Santo NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Espírito Santo NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

Venda, fornecimento e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas estarão proibidos em locais públicos ou de acesso público em todo o Maranhão das 0h às 20h deste domingo (25).

A determinação vale para qualquer tipo de bebida alcoólica e também para substâncias de efeitos semelhantes. A restrição inclui bares, restaurantes e outros estabelecimentos de acesso público. O descumprimento pode caracterizar crime de desobediência, além de resultar em penalidades administrativas e encaminhamento à autoridade policial.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Mato Grosso (TRE-MT) proibiu a venda, o fornecimento, a distribuição e o consumo de bebidas alcoólicas em estabelecimentos comerciais, locais públicos e espaços abertos ao público durante o segundo turno das Eleições Gerais de 2026.

A restrição valerá das 7h às 16h em todo o estado. A medida busca evitar confusões e manter a tranquilidade nos locais de votação. A proibição inclui o fornecimento gratuito de bebidas alcoólicas em bares, restaurantes e outros estabelecimentos, além de espaços públicos ou abertos ao público.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Mato Grosso do Sul (TRE-MS) definiu que não haverá Lei Seca no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições 2026 . Com a decisão, a venda e o consumo de bebidas alcoólicas em bares, restaurantes e estabelecimentos comerciais estão liberados em todos os municípios sul-mato-grossenses.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Minas Gerais (TRE-MG) anunciou que o estado NÃO terá Lei Seca durante as Eleições deste ano. O TRE-MG também fez o anúncio de medidas de segurança para o período.

A Polícia Civil do Pará divulgou as diretrizes para a aplicação da Lei Seca em todo o estado durante as Eleições 2026. As determinações estabelecem que estão proibidas , em todo o território paraense, comercialização e distribuição de álcool, bem como a realização de festas dançantes, shows, bailes e apresentações (públicas ou privadas) em clubes, casas de shows, bares e estabelecimentos similares.

A Lei Seca entra em vigor das 0h às 18h deste domingo (25), durante o segundo turno das Eleições 2026. A medida busca garantir a ordem pública, a segurança dos eleitores e a tranquilidade nos arredores das seções eleitorais.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral da Paraíba NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Paraná NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Pernambuco NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

Compra e venda de bebidas alcoólicas estão proibidas em todo o território estadual durante o segundo turno das Eleições de 2026 no Piauí. A proibição será válida da 0h às 18h do dia 4 de outubro, domingo. Anteriormente, a previsão era de 24 horas de restrição. Segundo a Secretaria de Segurança, o objetivo é preservar a ordem e a tranquilidade pública.

O Rio de Janeiro não terá Lei Seca durante as Eleições de 2026. A informação foi confirmada pela Secretaria de Estado Segurança Pública (Sesp). Com isso, não haverá restrição à venda e ao consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado nos dias de votação.

No Rio, a proibição da comercialização e do consumo de bebidas alcoólicas durante as eleições não é adotada desde 1996.

O Rio Grande do Norte não terá Lei Seca nas Eleições de 2026. Dessa forma, o consumo e a venda de bebidas alcoólicas no dia da votação serão permitidos no estado. A informação foi confirmada pelo secretário de Estado da Segurança Pública (Sesed) Coronel Francisco de Araújo.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Rio Grande do Sul NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

Até o momento, não foi identificada a edição de ato normativo pelo Governo de Rondônia estabelecendo proibição geral da venda de bebidas alcoólicas em razão das Eleições de 2026.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Roraima (TRE-RR) vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições. O tribunal não indicou a faixa de horário em que as restrições acontecerão.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Santa Catarina NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de São Paulo NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

O Tribunal Regional Eleitoral de Sergipe NÃO vai suspender a venda, distribuição e consumo de bebidas alcoólicas no estado durante o segundo turno das Eleições.

Tocantins: sem definição para todo o estado

No Tocantins, a decisão sobre a proibição ou não do consumo e venda de bebidas alcoólicas fica a cargo de juízes de diferentes zonas eleitorais. As resoluções não valem para todo o estado.

Na capital Palmas, a Justiça Eleitoral proibiu a venda, a distribuição e o consumo durante o segundo turno, começando a valer na meia-noite de domingo (25) e terminando às 17h. A restrição também vale para a região de Araguaína e Porto Nacional, onde começa às 18h do sábado (3) e termina às 18h do domingo. A medida também vale para os municípios de Brejinho de Nazaré, Ipueiras, Monte do Carmo, Porto Nacional, Santa Rita do Tocantins e Silvanópolis.

Os candidatos Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) disputam o segundo turno das eleições presidenciais neste domingo (25). O vencedor da disputa tomará posse em 5 de janeiro de 2027, conforme a nova regra estabelecida pela Constituição Federal.

Quando é a posse dos governadores em 2027?

Já os governadores eleitos nos 26 estados e no Distrito Federal tomam posse no dia seguinte, 6 de janeiro de 2027. Assim como o presidente da República, os governadores têm mandatos de quatro anos.

Por que a data da posse presidencial mudou?

As datas foram alteradas pela Emenda Constitucional nº 111, aprovada em setembro de 2021. Antes da mudança, as cerimônias eram realizadas em 1º de janeiro.

Esta será a primeira vez que a nova regra será aplicada às posses presidencial e dos governadores. Isso porque, embora a mudança tenha sido aprovada em 2021, as novas datas só passaram a valer para os eleitos a partir de 2026. Por isso, a posse de Lula em 2023 ainda ocorreu em 1º de janeiro.

Urna eletrônica completa 30 anos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Neste domingo (25), data do segundo turno das Eleições 2026 , os eleitores terão menos cargos para votar na urna eletrônica do que no primeiro turno. Em cinco estados, os eleitores também terão que escolher quem será o próximo governador.

A ordem de votação no segundo turno dependerá do estado ou município, já que nem todos os locais terão disputa para governador. Além disso, algumas cidades terão ainda eleições suplementares para prefeito ou plebiscitos.

Nos estados e municípios sem segundo turno para governador, eleição suplementar para prefeito ou plebiscito, os eleitores votarão apenas para presidente da República.

Nesse caso, será necessário digitar os dois números do candidato escolhido na urna eletrônica e confirmar o voto.

Presidente da República: digitar os dois números do candidato e confirmar o voto.

Ou seja, o voto para governador vem antes do voto para presidente. Para os dois cargos, o eleitor deverá digitar dois números na urna eletrônica.

articles.title: O que acontece se Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro empatarem no segundo turno? | G1
articles.standfirst: Legislação eleitoral brasileira estabelece um critério de desempate caso dois candidatos terminem a votação com exatamente o mesmo número de votos válidos.
articles.summary: Legislação eleitoral brasileira estabelece um critério de desempate caso dois candidatos terminem a votação com exatamente o mesmo número de votos válidos.
articles.body:
Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro na Globo — Foto: Lula (à esquerda) e Flávio Bolsonaro (à direita) disputam o 2º turno — Foto: Divulgação

Os brasileiros vão às urnas neste domingo (25) para escolher o próximo presidente da República. A disputa do segundo turno das Eleições 2026 acontece entre Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) . Mas o que acontece se os dois candidatos terminarem a votação com exatamente o mesmo número de votos?

A legislação eleitoral brasileira prevê um critério de desempate para essa situação: o candidato mais velho é considerado eleito. A regra está prevista no artigo 110 do Código Eleitoral.

Ou seja, em caso de empate absoluto entre os candidatos a presidência, Lula ganharia a disputa, já que tem 80 anos, enquanto Flávio tem 45.

Para que isso aconteça, porém, os dois candidatos precisariam receber exatamente a mesma quantidade de votos válidos. Uma diferença de apenas um voto já seria suficiente para definir o resultado da eleição.

O artigo 110 do Código Eleitoral estabelece que, em caso de empate, será considerado eleito o candidato mais idoso.

Se Lula tiver mais votos válidos: será eleito presidente.

Se Flávio Bolsonaro tiver mais votos válidos: será eleito presidente.

Se os dois tiverem exatamente a mesma quantidade de votos válidos: o critério de idade será utilizado para desempatar a disputa.

A Constituição Federal também estabelece, no artigo 77, que a eleição presidencial é decidida pela maioria dos votos válidos.

Votos brancos e nulos contam para o desempate?

Não. Segundo a Justiça Eleitoral, apenas os votos válidos são considerados na apuração para definir o vencedor das eleições.

Isso significa que os votos em branco e os votos nulos são desconsiderados na contagem. Eles não são transferidos para nenhum candidato e também não interferem no critério de desempate.

Por exemplo, se Lula e Flávio receberem 60 milhões de votos válidos cada, haverá um empate absoluto, independentemente da quantidade de votos brancos e nulos registrados.

Empate técnico é a mesma coisa que empate nas urnas?

Não. Embora os termos sejam parecidos, eles representam situações diferentes.

O empate técnico acontece quando a diferença entre os candidatos em uma pesquisa eleitoral está dentro da margem de erro do levantamento. Isso significa que, considerando a incerteza estatística, a pesquisa não permite estabelecer com segurança qual dos candidatos tem maior intenção de voto.

Já o empate nas urnas ocorre quando os dois candidatos recebem exatamente a mesma quantidade de votos válidos na eleição.

Diferentemente das pesquisas eleitorais, a apuração dos votos não utiliza margem de erro. Por isso, mesmo que a diferença entre Lula e Flávio seja de apenas um voto, o candidato que receber mais votos válidos será eleito.

articles.body:
Former President Barack Obama poked fun at President Trump’s various Washington, D.C.-area renovation projects during a campaign stop in Cleveland, Ohio, where he was stumping for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown.

In his speech, Obama zeroed in on the changes President Trump has made to the White House during his second term, saying he believes Trump is more focused on renovating the White House than on the issues voters care about.

“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of Trump’s over $900 million worth of White House construction efforts. “What’s with the gold? … He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

This isn’t the first time Obama has ribbed Trump for his gold-heavy redecoration of the White House, previously doing so on Larry David’s HBO Max show “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness.”

The former president’s attacks did not stop with the White House. Obama went on to blast Trump’s other renovation projects as well.

The Democrat singled out Trump’s original 2016 message to “drain the swamp,” a call to shake up the Washington establishment, jokingly drawing comparisons between the adage and his attempted renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

After the White House unveiled the newly-renovated pool in June, onlookers began to spot a growth of green algae in the water and the peeling of newly installed “American flag blue” base paint. After months of renovations and a heated legal battle surrounding vandalism allegations, Trump said Friday the pool is 85 percent done with the refilling process.

“Remember that whole thing about drain the swamp? The only thing that got drained was the Reflecting Pool in the National Mall after some no-bid contract got it all messed up,” Obama said.

articles.title: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida
articles.summary: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday, saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally.
articles.body: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday, saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally. Trump and first lady Melania Trump arrived at their West Palm Beach polling location at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office together after the president spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Trump has been criticized in the past for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots. Asked if he voted the party line, Trump, who was wearing an “I Voted” sticker, said, “Very much so.” Speaking to reporters at the poll site, Trump again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12. Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. As for the war in Iran, he said, “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.” Melania Trump, who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine. “We will see,” she told reporters. In Florida, Trump has endorsed Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. He has also campaigned for Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, who is running to fill the last two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s former Senate term against progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon.

articles.title: Obama rallies rapturous Michigan crowd for El-Sayed: ‘He’ll finish the job we started’
articles.summary: Former president speaks to crowd of thousands in support of Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate and Democratic ticket
articles.body:
Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was "fighting for change, real change, that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket", as he threw his weight behind the Democratic Senate candidate and the rest of the ticket on the first day of early voting in Michigan.

Obama said in front of thousands of onlookers at Cass technical high school in Detroit that El-Sayed would "finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American".

The former president headlined the rally for El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate, and secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, the party's candidate for governor, at an evening event to "get out the vote".

He accused Donald Trump of "enriching himself and his family", and said the administration had set a "culture … at the top" of taking favors. "Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this," he said.

The rally came on the first day of Michigan's early voting period, with the general election on 3 November. It was also Obama's first weekend of in-person campaigning during the midterms, which started in Cleveland, Ohio, earlier in the day to stump for the former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton earlier in the weekend. He issued similarly scathing remarks aimed at the White House and the GOP .

The Detroit stop is Obama's first public show of support for El-Sayed, who emerged from a bitter August primary in which the former president stayed on the sidelines. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health official, beat the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens who was riding on the backing of the Democratic establishment and pro-Israel organizations.

Obama was on the offensive against the administration, mocking the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, as "laser-focused" on the "jawline and testosterone levels of our troops", asking: "How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?"

On tariffs, Obama said Trump was toughest on "that well-known evil empire", referring to Canada, a few minutes' drive from Detroit across the bridge. "These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup," he said.

He even took a jab at Trump's attempts to renovate the White House. "He should be on HGTV," Obama said of the many renovations in Washington, including the White House ballroom and the Rose Garden. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

Questions had hung over whether Obama would back El-Sayed at all. El-Sayed, a champion of Medicare for All, had at one point called the Affordable Care Act, Obama's signature domestic achievement, an incremental fix. The two men spoke by phone after the primary, and El-Sayed has since called Obama a mentor figure.

El-Sayed has the most ground to make up in Wayne county, where Detroit is the county seat, after Stevens beat him there by about 51% to 45% in the August primaries. Obama last campaigned in Detroit – which is more than three-quarters Black – in October 2024 for Kamala Harris, and Harris herself appeared with El-Sayed in Detroit last month.

Republicans have not held a Michigan Senate seat in 25 years, but the party sees the seat as one of its better pickup chances nationwide. El-Sayed faces Mike Rogers, a former congressman endorsed by Donald Trump who lost a 2024 Senate matchup against Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point. The Cook Political Report rates this race a toss-up.

Slotkin, a featured speaker at the rally, told the crowd that "Michigan believes in electing fighters". And when it came to any disagreements she may have with El-Sayed, she said: "It's OK because we agree on so much more."

"We're putting a check and balance on Donald Trump in the White House," she said.

A Marist poll of likely voters statewide conducted in mid-October put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, within the margin of error. RealClearPolitics's average had El-Sayed ahead by about 2.6 points in a similar timeframe.

Trump has attacked El-Sayed throughout the campaign, calling him a "jihadist", pointing to his middle name and alleging that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed strongly denies, and has created one of the most viral moments of the year. El-Sayed has also faced a barrage of criticism from the establishment wing of the Democratic party over his appearances with leftwing streamer Hasan Piker .

Trump is due in the state himself on Sunday, when he will hold a rally for Michigan Republicans in Port Huron, on the Canadian border. The city said it will be the first presidential visit to St Clair county.

If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim and first Egyptian American in the US Senate. Benson faces the Republican congressman John James; a James win would make him Michigan's first Black governor.

Turning to the disagreements between them, Obama acknowledged that some people had pointed out that El-Sayed "didn't like some things you did as president". "We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue," he said. "You know who else doesn't agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama."

"We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society," Obama said, "and that the system's not just run for those at the top."

articles.title: Ukraine's Starlink restored as Elon Musk claims Kyiv violated terms of service 'to kill people'
articles.summary: Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms of service by using the civilian system for deadly drone strikes, saying the loophole was closed.
articles.body: Elon Musk on Saturday continued to defend Starlink after Ukraine faced more than a week of speed restrictions that disrupted its war effort against Russia, saying SpaceX has done more to defend the country than any other private company "by far," while accusing the country of using the technology in violation of its terms of service "to kill people." "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X, claiming that Ukraine had "violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week." He explained that Starshield is a different system controlled by the U.S. government. "What they decide to do is up to them." ELON MUSK BLAMES TRUMP, US MILITARY FOR SPACEX RESTRICTIONS UKRAINE WARNS COULD HAVE DEADLY CONSEQUENCES "Starlink remains critical to the defense of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now," he wrote in response to an X post that stated Starlink is "not a weapons system." "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," he added. Musk said that Starlink was crucial at the beginning of the war because it was the only means of communication that couldn’t be "destroyed or jammed by Russia. "SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR," he claimed. "That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict. May you burn in hell. End of story." Last week, Musk blamed the issue on the U.S. military. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the SpaceX, Tesla and X CEO wrote in a post. UKRAINE SHOWED TRUMP HOW EASILY AN ENEMY COULD CRIPPLE AN AI POWERHOUSE A source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital that Ukraine received no advance warning before the restrictions took effect overnight, despite relying on the service under arrangements contracted through the U.S. government until May 15, 2027. Ukrainian forces discovered the change after experiencing connectivity problems and contacting SpaceX customer support. They were told Starshield service would be restricted on platforms traveling at speeds of 100 mph or higher, the source said. Musk did not say whether President Donald Trump, War Secretary Pete Hegseth or another U.S. official personally authorized the new restriction or explain why it was imposed. Trump told reporters on Saturday that he had spoken to Musk about the issue, but wouldn’t elaborate. UKRAINE REGAINS CRITICAL STARLINK SERVICE AFTER RESTRICTIONS DISRUPT DRONE OPERATIONS Ukraine's Ministry of Defense announced Saturday that it had regained broader access to Starlink, with connections remaining stable at speeds of 250 mph. It remains unclear what led to the slowdown in service, with Ukraine having accused both Trump and Musk of being behind it, and comes after renewed hope for Ukraine and Russia to reach a resolution in the war. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Hegseth have denied that the U.S. government was responsible for slowing Ukraine's Starlink service. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told "Fox & Friends" this week he would be open to ending the war by freezing the fighting along the current front lines. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House, SpaceX, along with the War and State departments for comment. Fox News' James Cirrone contributed to this report.

articles.title: Obama seeks to shore up Abdul El-Sayed with Black voters at Michigan rally
articles.summary: Former President Barack Obama rallied for Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday as the bitterly fought contest could come down to the city’s substantial Black vote.
articles.body: Former President Barack Obama rallied for Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday as the bitterly fought contest could come down to the city’s substantial Black vote. “We’re clear about the choice in this election,” Obama said. “Abdul is fighting for change, real change, change that will bring an end to this war. Change that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket. Change that will finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American.” “You hear people say this is somehow radical,” Obama continued. “What is radical about that?” The former president, who rallied earlier Saturday in Cleveland, was joined by El-Sayed, gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson and downballot Democrats less than two weeks before Election Day. Like his speech earlier in the day, Obama lambasted President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans for “broken promises” made during their 2024 campaigns and criticized Trump’s handling of the Iran War and tariffs, both of which he said have had an outsize effect on Michigan. “Does anybody really think this guy is spending that much time thinking deeply on these issues? I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he is very focused on home renovation. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of Trump’s extensive changes to the White House. “You remember — roll back the tape, ‘We’re gonna drain the swamp,’” Obama added. “The only thing they drained is the reflecting pool on the National Mall because some no-bid contract got it all messed up.” The Black vote has become a focus in the race as both El-Sayed and his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., have sought to improve their standing with the critical electorate. Detroit, a city where 75% of the population is Black, is crucial to statewide victories for Michigan Democrats. In the Democratic primary, El-Sayed underperformed there compared to his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. Speaking ahead of the former president, El-Sayed excoriated Rogers for appearing this Sunday with Trump while contrasting his presidency with Obama’s. “Trump got us into a war we’ve got no business fighting,” El-Sayed said. “President Obama, he contained the nuclear threat without war. Trump’s tariffs costing autoworkers their livelihoods. President Obama, he made sure that they didn’t lose their jobs in the worst financial crisis in a century.” An epidemiologist, El-Sayed has leaned on his experience as health director in both Detroit and Wayne County while touting support from prominent Black Democrats, including former Vice President Kamala Harris; Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga.; Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass.; and Michigan Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist to help him make his case. “Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said. “Abdul was born here. He was raised here. Parents in the auto industry … Captain of his high school football and lacrosse and wrestling teams. I mean, he’s just a jock. You see those big guns. That’s why he wears those T-shirts.” Polls have consistently forecast a tight race between El-Sayed and Rogers, showing El-Sayed with a substantial edge over Rogers with Black voters. But the margin matters. A recent YouGov survey of likely general election voters found El-Sayed winning 84% of the Black vote, with Rogers taking 11% — roughly the same spread that Michigan exit polls showed in 2024, when Harris narrowly lost the state to Trump in the presidential election. A Fox News poll of likely voters in late September measured Rogers’ support among Black voters at 22%. NBC News visited an early voting location in Detroit on Saturday, ahead of Obama’s rally. Voters who spoke with NBC News said they were casting ballots for El-Sayed. “I’ll admit that I’ve skipped it before,” Tony Gooden, a Detroit voter, said in an interview of having not voted in prior midterm elections. Gooden added that he felt it was important to vote this fall because of “the state of the economy, the state of our country.” “I feel like somebody needs to put a rein on what’s going on in Washington,” said Gooden. “So I can either sit back on my couch and complain, or I can get on and do something about it.” Mary Waters, a member of the Detroit City Council who backed Stevens in the Democratic primary, said she is not yet committed to either candidate but expressed warmth toward Rogers. She said that skepticism of El-Sayed may stem less from a personal dislike of him and more from tense relationships between the Arab American and Black communities in Detroit. “I don’t think that President Obama himself even understands the racial divides, the class divides, in the city. He does not live here,” Waters said when asked about the impact Obama’s appearance could have, acknowledging that some of her constituents may be swayed by Obama’s pitch. In a recent interview with The Root, an online publication that covers Black news and culture, El-Sayed acknowledged the tensions Waters highlighted. “Most of that spending was spending intended to break my relationship with the Black community,” El-Sayed said of money spent opposing him during the Democratic primary. “And unfortunately, you know, it was not that hard to break, because for too many Black Detroiters, in particular, their experience with somebody who looks like me is not a good one.” “You go into a gas station, you go to a party store, you’re being talked at from behind bulletproof glass,” he continued. “If you’re a woman, you’re being catcalled. … I’ve always tried to be on the right side of that. But I also understand that, like, if that’s your experience with somebody whose name is like mine, that leaves a terrible taste in your mouth.” Gilchrist, meanwhile, told NBC News he thinks little of Rogers’ attempts to woo Black voters and believes Obama’s rally would help unify the party. “He occupies a singular place in our consciousness as Black Americans, and so his voice matters, and his perspective matters,” Gilchrist said. “I do think that that will be incredibly helpful in terms of letting folks know that this is an opportunity for them to mobilize and to make something happen to have the right senator from Michigan.” El-Sayed, though, has previously expressed criticism of Obama, saying he fell short of delivering change. He has explained his thinking in the run-up to Saturday’s rally. “Do you love your dad? Do you agree with everything your dad has ever done?” El-Sayed said after his Grand Rapids debate with Rogers on Oct. 8. “It’s a normal thing to love somebody, to really appreciate all that they’ve done, and to say, ‘Hey, here’s some things I would have done differently.’ But they still did some important things to create opportunity for you. There is no world in which I get to run for office without somebody like President Obama.” Obama addressed the past criticism on Saturday. “Abdul shares my values of wanting everybody to get healthcare,” he said. “He shares my values that if you work hard every day, you should have a living wage, and you should be able, if you’re a young person starting a family, to be able to buy a house that you can afford, and that you shouldn’t have to pay six bucks every time you fill up the tank of gas to get to work. We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society, and that the system’s not just run for those at the top.” Republicans blasted the rally Saturday, painting El-Sayed as an extremist. “The idea that Barack Obama and Jocelyn Benson would share the stage with” El-Sayed “shows that the Democrat Party is not interested in fixing the issues facing Michigan families, and will always put politics over people,” Republican Governors Association communications director Kollin Crompton said in a statement. Speaking ahead of Obama, Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., sought to explain how the battleground state could potentially send both her, a center-left Democrat, and the progressive El-Sayed to the Senate. “The difference these days under this president is not between progressive versus moderate,” she said. “It is between team fight and team flight.”

articles.title: ACLU, Common Cause file motion against DOJ over Alaska election certification block
articles.summary: Nonprofit watchdog group Common Cause, represented by attorneys from American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), has filed a motion to intervene in the Justice Department’s lawsuit over Alaska’s Senate election. The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit Thursday claiming that the presence of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) could…
articles.body:
Nonprofit watchdog group Common Cause, represented by attorneys from American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), has filed a motion to intervene in the Justice Department’s lawsuit over Alaska’s Senate election.

The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit Thursday claiming that the presence of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) could give Democrat Mary Peltola an unfair advantage in the upcoming Senate election.

The motion brought by Common Cause and the ACLU aims to stop the DOJ “from blocking Alaska’s Senate election results,” according to a press release sent Saturday by Common Cause.

“Common Cause’s filing argues that DOJ’s attempt to interfere and disrupt Alaska’s election is baseless, and that the federal government has no authority to bring this case,” the release said.

“The Trump administration is trying to lay the groundwork to reject election results because they are desperate to control our elections,” said Virginia Kase Solomon, president and CEO of Common Cause in the release.

The Justice Department’s lawsuit, which President Trump has said he directed to be filed , claimed Daniel J. Sullivan entered the Senate race “as a Republican with the intention of misleading” the incumbent senator’s supporters.

“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” the filing reads.

In a social media post on Saturday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said with this lawsuit, the department is not trying to stop the certification of Alaska’s election, but is seeking “to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead.”

Saturday’s motion lists Alaska voters Risé Roy and Jan Jakub Grzeda and the League of Women Voters of Alaska along with Common Cause as the proposed intervenors.

“Proposed Intervenors have a strong interest in the certification of free and fair election results in the Alaska Senate contest,” the filing from the nonprofit organization read. “The relief the federal government seeks risks disenfranchising Alaska residents entirely.”

articles.title: Trump announces at a Georgia campaign rally that Audi will build a new auto factory in the state
articles.summary: (AP) — President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that Audi will build an automobile plant in Georgia as he tries to deliver on his promise to bolster Amer...
articles.body:
PERRY, Ga. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Saturday announced that Audi will build an automobile plant in Georgia as he tries to deliver on his promise to bolster American manufacturing in the final days before the midterm elections.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, where he sought to boost Republican candidates, Trump said Audi — the German luxury brand owned by Volkswagen — would commit $4.2 billion in nearby Macon to begin construction on a plant that will produce 200,000 cars a year.

"Think of that. 200,000 cars a year. That's incredible," Trump said, crediting his aggressive and unpopular tariff policies for the company's decision to build the plant.

The announcement seemed timed to offer a last-minute boost to Republican candidates in the battleground state, including Rep. Mike Collins, who is trying to unseat Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Trump has spent October campaigning in reliably Republican states as the party tries to hold onto its majorities in the House and Senate. Trump won Georgia in 2024 after losing it in 2020.

Trump was joined on stage by Gernot Döllner, the chairman of the board of management at Audi, who said the plant would be producing "our biggest and most premium SUVs."

"This is a long-term investment, because we believe in the American market," he said.

Audi, in a news release, said the plant — its first in Georgia — would create approximately 4,500 jobs and that construction was scheduled to begin in 2027, with production beginning in the early 2030s.

Republicans are bracing for losses in the Nov. 3 midterm elections as they contend with an unpopular president and an electorate that is angry over high costs and the ongoing war in Iran.

At the rally, Rick Jackson , the Republican candidate for Georgia governor, thanked Trump for the plans.

"Thank you on behalf of Georgia for putting the biggest economic deal in Georgia history right here today," he said.

articles.title: James Fishback allegedly blocked from entering Florida Republicans’ rally
articles.summary: Former gubernatorial candidate James Fishback (R) said he was stopped from entering a Get Out the Vote rally in Clearwater, Fla. hosted by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) on Saturday. Fishback said him and wife were told that he was “not welcome here” when trying to enter the venue, local news station CBS 12 reported.…
articles.body:
Former gubernatorial candidate James Fishback (R) said he was stopped from entering a Get Out the Vote rally in Clearwater, Fla. hosted by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) on Saturday.

Fishback said him and wife were told that he was “not welcome here” when trying to enter the venue, local news station CBS 12 reported .

“I have attended political events featuring Donald Trump, Barack Obama, George W. Bush, Bernie Sanders, and I’ve never had any issues. It is disgraceful that Byron Donalds would threaten to arrest us for attending a political event open to the public,” Fishback said according to the report.

Gates McGavick, who handles communications for Donalds’ campaign, posted on X saying “this is a lie. It wasn’t even Byron’s event. He did not kick anyone out, much less threaten anyone with arrest.”

The rally, hosted by Luna, listed Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) and Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) as special guests, according to the CBS 12 report.

The Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office told the news station that Luna’s staff advised detectives that Fishback was not welcome, however detectives did not threaten him with arrest.

Earlier this year, Fishback said his campaign was banned from Waffle House restaurants across Florida, after he announced in January that he planned to visit every Waffle House in the state to connect with voters over “hot coffee and warm waffles.”

Fishback, who lost his gubernational bid to Donalds, has previously been criticized for alleged inappropriate behavior and racist comments while on the campaign trail.

articles.title: Democrats ask judge to dismiss Trump administration’s challenge to Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: Attorneys for Alaska’s Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola and Senate Democrats filed a motion Friday urging a federal judge to drop the Trump administration’s lawsuit that seeks to block the results of the upcoming election if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses.
articles.body: Attorneys for Alaska’s Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola and Senate Democrats filed a motion Friday urging a federal judge to drop the Trump administration’s lawsuit that seeks to block the results of the upcoming election if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses. The motion, filed on behalf of Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, called the lawsuit filed by the Justice Department “an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections.” “This case directly threatens both Proposed Intervenors’ interests by demanding that defendants refuse to certify the election if, and only if, Peltola wins,” the filing said. “It is part of a nationwide attack on free elections by the federal government, which the DSCC has fought at every turn.” The Trump administration filed suit against election officials in Alaska Thursday, arguing that candidate Dan J. Sullivan Jr.’s appearance on the ballot could mislead those who wish to vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan’s re-election. The lawsuit came after President Donald Trump repeatedly complained about both the incumbent being threatened by a man with the same name and the state’s use of ranked-choice voting. “I am very concerned about the Dan S. Sullivan Race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska in that it is totally confusing,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post Wednesday. “It’s ridiculous that the Court didn’t stop this SCAM.” The DOJ’s lawsuit asks the court to block the Alaska Senate results from being certified if Dan S. Sullivan does not win the election, and if “had all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.” The filing from Peltola and Senate Democrats pushes back against this request, stating that “the Department of Justice’s assumption that every voter who casts a vote for Dan J. Sullivan really meant to vote for Senator Sullivan is insulting to voters and irreconcilable with Alaska’s ranked choice voting procedures and the ballot’s clear differentiation between the two candidates.” “Alaskans for Mary and DSCC are entitled to intervene as of right to defend against the Department of Justice’s extraordinary assault,” the motion said. “And there is reason to doubt that the existing defendants will vigorously defend against DOJ’s demands, given their effort to exclude Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot earlier this year.” After Dan J. Sullivan Jr. was removed from the ballot in June after election officials decided his candidacy was “not in good faith,” a judge in Alaska overturned the decision later that month, validating his campaign. Trump has claimed that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. is only running because “Democrats put him up as a matter of confusion,” calling his candidacy “corrupt.” Dan J. Sullivan Jr. has denied the allegations. NBC News reported in July that federal and state investigators were looking into whether Dan J. Sullivan Jr. could be part of a conspiracy to confuse voters, according to two people who had knowledge of the situation. The DOJ’s lawsuit comes less than two weeks ahead of Election Day and after the state has begun early voting. The court has not yet set a hearing date for the suit. Legal and election experts told NBC News that the DOJ’s case is on shaky ground. As U.S. elections are run and certified by state and local officials, rather than the federal government, the law limits the Justice Department’s role in elections. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the Alaska Senate contest as a “toss-up.” The race marks a critical opportunity for Democrats to take a seat from Republicans as they vie for control of the Senate.

images.caption: Dan Sullivan; Mary Peltola
